AMD Showcases 6th Gen AMD EPYC Processors to Lead Next Era of AI and Enterprise Computing :: Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (AMD)
Press Release
AMD Showcases 6th Gen AMD EPYC Processors to Lead Next Era of AI and Enterprise Computing
November 10, 2026 12:00 pm EST
Download as PDF
News Highlights:
6
th
Gen AMD EPYC SP7 CPU-based platforms are now shipping from leading server OEMs and ODMs.
6
th
Gen EPYC CPUs are expected to power cloud instances across all major, global cloud service providers, with recent announcements from Microsoft Azure and OCI showcasing leadership agent orchestration, concurrent agent sandboxes, as well as web and enterprise applications.
Powered by the new AMD “Zen 6” architecture, 6
th
Gen EPYC CPUs deliver a broad portfolio of workload-optimized server CPUs spanning agentic AI, enterprise, cloud computing, HPC and general-purpose computing.
SANTA CLARA, Calif., Nov. 10, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- AMD (NASDAQ: AMD) today announced the general availability of the 6
th
Gen AMD EPYC™ server SP7 processors, based on the new “Zen 6” architecture, extending its historical server CPU performance leadership as AI creates new demands across the data center. Systems powered by the new CPUs are shipping from leading server vendors, and cloud instances from Microsoft Azure and OCI will be generally available soon.
Across five generations, AMD EPYC processors have repeatedly raised the standard for server CPU performance, energy efficiency and platform choice, culminating in 5
th
Gen AMD EPYC™ processors becoming the fastest-ramping and highest-volume EPYC generation in AMD history. Now, 6
th
Gen AMD EPYC server CPUs extend AMD CPU leadership, running AI agents, accelerated infrastructure and critical enterprise applications, helping customers expand computing capacity that runs their businesses.
More:
AMD Launches 6th Gen AMD EPYC Embedded Processors, Extending CPU Leadership
(News) |
AMD In Depth: EPYC ‘Venice’
(Press Kit, Videos, Photos)
“AI is significantly expanding the role of the CPU across every layer of the data center,” said Dan McNamara, senior vice president and general manager, Compute and Enterprise AI, AMD. “With 6
th
Gen AMD EPYC, customers can standardize on the proven x86 foundation while choosing a workload-optimized solution to run more agents, keep accelerated infrastructure fed, and power the business-critical applications they depend on.”
World’s Best Server CPU Portfolio for the Modern Data Center
6
th
Gen AMD EPYC is the world’s best server CPU portfolio,
i
providing a workload-optimized stack that delivers leadership performance across a diversity of applications while improving infrastructure economics and preserving the flexibility of the broad x86 ecosystem.
Agentic AI adds even more diversity to a data center as a single workflow can run agents, call models, retrieve data, execute code and interact with the databases and applications enterprises already depend on. The 6
th
Gen AMD EPYC portfolio is designed for that reality, matching CPU density, frequency, bandwidth and efficiency to each job while preserving one common software, security and operational foundation. That workload-optimized approach delivers advantages across critical areas including agentic AI, enterprise services and rack-scale solutions.
Power More Enterprise and Cloud Services:
The 6th Gen AMD EPYC™ 9996 CPU is the world’s best general-purpose processor, delivering leadership performance, performance per CPU watt, performance per CPU dollar and performance per socket. An AMD EPYC 9996 CPU-based system delivers up to 3.7x more performance compared with an Nvidia Vera CPU-based system and up to 2.2x the performance and 2.0x the performance per dollar of an Intel® Xeon® 6980P system.
ii
For customers, that can translate into more applications, transactions and users supported by each server, helping create capacity for new workloads within existing data center power and footprint limitations.
Lead Across Every Tier of Agentic AI:
Agentic AI infrastructure spans three distinct CPU roles – general-purpose services, GPU host nodes, and agent sandboxes – and 6th Gen AMD EPYC provides a workload-optimized processor for each. High-frequency host-node processors, with up to 5.3 GHz, can deliver up to 1.8x the LLM output throughput of previous generation EPYC processors
iii
and high-density AMD EPYC processors can provide up to ~3.3x agents-per-CPU-watt advantage over Nvidia Vera and ~2.5x over Intel Xeon 6980P for hosting agent sandboxes.
iv
Additionally, for agent sandboxes, AMD EPYC 9996 CPU-based servers can support an estimated ~1.18x as many agents per rack within the same 35 kilowatt power envelope as systems using default power-management settings.
v
The competitive choice is increasingly straightforward. With 6th Gen AMD EPYC, customers do not have to settle for a one-size-fits-all CPU in a data center that is anything but uniform. AMD EPYC delivers the performance, choice and ecosystem support needed to move AI from answers to action and prepare for what comes next.
From the Server to Rack-Scale AI
6th Gen AMD EPYC extends its leadership from individual servers to AMD Helion™ agentic AI racks, giving customers three deployment options matched to how and where they operate: AMD Helion Liquid, designed to sit side-by-side with AMD Helios™ rackscale solution in large-scale agentic AI deployments, for maximum agent density; AMD Helion Air for expanding agent capacity within existing air-cooled data centers; and AMD Helion Air Inference for combining CPU execution and local GPU inference in one rack. AMD has worked across the server ecosystem to help develop the high-density AMD Helion rack with some configurations reaching up to 73,728 threads in one rack, delivering the most agents available in a rack. Customers can choose the balance of CPU and GPU capacity, cooling and connectivity that fits their infrastructure as agent demand grows.
Broad Ecosystem Support and Availability
Systems powered by 6th Gen AMD EPYC server processors are shipping from leading server vendors:
Meta
is working with AMD as a lead customer and has been validating 6th Gen AMD EPYC CPU-based platforms as the companies prepare for deployment at scale.
Microsoft
Azure is bringing 6th Gen AMD EPYC to customers across the AI infrastructure stack, with Azure HDv2 now in preview for AI data processing, agentic AI and HPC; Azure HXv2 for EDA and technical computing; and Azure ND MI455X v7, based on AMD Helios, for production-scale AI inference.
AMD recently shared updates to its multigeneration collaboration with
Oracle Cloud Infrastructure
(OCI). OCI Compute E7 cloud compute instances will be powered by 6th Gen AMD EPYC server processors, supporting enterprise applications and the CPU services surrounding AI models.
With 6th Gen AMD EPYC, AMD is extending five generations of server CPU leadership into the agentic AI era; delivering more compute, better economics and more choice from the server to the rack. Across enterprise, cloud, HPC and AI infrastructure, EPYC provides a broad portfolio built for the workloads customers run today and what comes next.

AMD (NASDAQ: AMD) drives innovation in high-performance and AI computing to solve the world’s most important challenges. AMD EPYC Expands Its Leadership at the Foundation of AI :: Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (AMD)
Press Release
AMD EPYC Expands Its Leadership at the Foundation of AI
November 09, 2026 8:00 am EST
Download as PDF
5th Gen AMD EPYC processors power Google Cloud TPU 8tx host infrastructure, helping enterprises protect sensitive AI models
News Highlights:
5th Gen AMD EPYC server CPUs power the host foundation for Google Cloud TPU 8tx, the first cloud Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) system with hardware-enforced confidential computing.
AMD EPYC processors enable protection of sensitive AI models and data, combining host processing, security capabilities and x86 software compatibility.
AMD EPYC processors are the host CPU of choice across more than 10 leading hyperscalers and frontier AI labs, spanning GPUs and custom AI accelerator ASICs.
SANTA CLARA, Calif., Nov.  09, 2026  (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- AMD (NASDAQ: AMD) today announced that 5th Gen AMD EPYC™ processors are powering the host infrastructure for Google Cloud TPU 8tx, the first cloud Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) system to deliver hardware-enforced confidential computing. The expanded collaboration between the companies combines AMD EPYC™ CPU performance, AMD Infinity Guard security capabilities and x86 software compatibility with Google Cloud TPU AI acceleration to help enterprises deploy inference, fine-tuning and reinforcement learning workloads.
1
With Google Cloud’s confidential computing architecture on TPU 8tx supported by 5th Gen AMD EPYC host processors, organizations can run their most sensitive AI workloads at scale in the cloud without compromising on data protection.
The deployment extends the role of AMD EPYC processors as a foundation for accelerated AI infrastructure. Across systems built with GPUs and custom accelerators, AMD EPYC CPUs are the choice for host processing – preparing data, coordinating workloads and managing communication with accelerators. With TPU 8tx, AMD and Google Cloud bring those capabilities together with hardware-rooted security to address a critical requirement for production AI: protecting data while it is in use.
“The most capable AI systems need a CPU foundation that can match the demands of the accelerators they host,” said Dan McNamara, senior vice president and general manager, Compute and Enterprise AI, AMD. “Across generations of EPYC, we have built leadership capabilities in the performance, memory bandwidth and I/O that keep accelerated systems productive, backed by years of engineering collaboration with the world’s leading cloud providers. Our work with Google Cloud brings that strength to TPU 8tx, helping customers scale AI with the performance and protection their most important workloads demand.”
“When teams move AI agents into production, they need confidence that their data and intellectual property stay private, even from the underlying infrastructure,” said Mark Lohmeyer, vice president and general manager for AI and Computing Infrastructure, Google Cloud. “By pairing 5th Gen AMD EPYC processors with our 8th-generation TPU architecture inside the AI Hypercomputer, we are bringing hardware-enforced confidential computing to cloud TPUs for the first time. Customers get silicon-level data protection alongside the low-latency performance needed for modern reasoning models.”
Enabling Confidential AI with AMD EPYC Processors
In TPU 8tx systems, 5th Gen AMD EPYC processors manage workload orchestration, data preparation and high-throughput communication with TPU accelerators. The system utilizes the AMD Secure Encrypted Virtualization (SEV) capabilities in the AMD EPYC CPU, which together with the TPU, extends confidential computing protection beyond the CPU to connected accelerators, helping protect sensitive data as it moves among them.
Verifying an accelerator’s identity and security configuration before granting it direct access to protected memory helps customer prompts, model weights and intermediate data remain encrypted in CPU memory and in transit among the host and accelerators, with hardware isolation during accelerator execution. These protections help enterprises use sensitive information with confidence in reasoning and agentic AI applications.
AMD EPYC processors also underpin the broader Google Cloud confidential computing portfolio: AMD SEV technologies help protect workloads across Confidential VMs, Confidential GKE, Confidential Space, Confidential Managed Service for Apache Spark, and Confidential Dataflow. TPU 8tx extends that collaboration to confidential AI acceleration.
A Proven Host CPU Foundation Across AI Architectures
As hyperscalers, frontier labs and model providers build increasingly specialized AI infrastructure, CPU selection remains central to system performance and deployment. Accelerators depend on host processors to supply data, schedule work and connect AI workloads with the applications and services around them. AMD EPYC processors are the host CPU of choice for more than 10 leading hyperscalers and frontier AI labs, spanning GPUs and custom AI accelerator ASICs.
AMD EPYC processors support this role across systems using AMD Instinct™ GPUs, Nvidia GPUs and custom silicon. This breadth gives customers a proven CPU platform across accelerator choices, supported by the established x86 software ecosystem.
Building on Generations of AMD and Google Cloud Collaborations
AMD and Google Cloud have collaborated across multiple generations of EPYC processors, supporting general-purpose, compute-intensive, storage-intensive and accelerated workloads leading up to current Google Cloud Compute Engine C4D, N4D, H4D, Z4D and G4 virtual machines. The companies have also worked together for years on security technology at the corporate level, including deep reviews of AMD security processor firmware by Google security experts.
With TPU 8tx, this expanded collaboration helps enterprises run modern reasoning and agentic AI workloads in production without compromising on data protection.

Faster Scientific Simulations with New FP64 Algorithms in NVIDIA cuBLAS

By
Cole Brower
,
Peter Caday
,
Vamsi Sripathi

Rob Parrish

Ed Hohenstein

AI-Generated Summary
CUDA Toolkit 13.4.2
introduces Ozaki-II and 2M algorithms that accelerate double-precision GEMM on integer Tensor Cores while preserving full FP64 accuracy.
Ozaki-II reduces the number of integer multiplications compared to Ozaki-I by using the Chinese Remainder Theorem, and the 2M method cuts complex matrix multiplication from four real multiplications to two.
DGEMM with Ozaki-II runs 5.5x faster than native FP64 on NVIDIA VR NVL72 and 3.9x faster on NVIDIA GB200, while ZGEMM with the 2M algorithm achieves a 5x speedup over native CFP64 on NVIDIA GB200.
CCSD quantum chemistry calculations using Ozaki-II DGEMM deliver 2x and 1.4x end-to-end speedups on NVIDIA VR NVL72 and NVIDIA GB200 in full FP64 precision, and 5x and 3.5x in mixed-precision mode.
BerkeleyGW materials science simulations using Ozaki-II 2M ZGEMM achieve 6.6x and 3.9x speedups over native ZGEMM on NVIDIA VR NVL72 and NVIDIA GB200 respectively.
NVIDIA Rubin GPUs introduce the TI16 numeric format and tcgen05.mma instruction, further accelerating Ozaki-I and Ozaki-II computations.
Next Steps
Download and install the latest
NVIDIA CUDA Toolkit
to access the new cuBLAS algorithms.
Read the
floating point emulation section of the cuBLAS documentation
for API details including cublasSetEmulationStrategy and manual mantissa bit control.
Explore the
cuBLAS Emulation samples on GitHub
to evaluate gains on your own workloads.
Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.
Learn more
Many scientific simulations, from molecular chemistry to materials science, spend the majority of their execution time computing high-precision dense general matrix multiplications (GEMM). These operations are called DGEMM for real 64-bit floating-point numbers and ZGEMM for complex 64-bit floating-point numbers. cuBLAS is widely used by HPC and AI applications to accelerate GEMM and other Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms (BLAS) on NVIDIA GPUs. Rapid advances in lower-precision hardware have motivated exploration of a new class of algorithms that deliver full double-precision results on the faster integer Tensor Cores.
With CUDA Toolkit 13.4.2, cuBLAS no longer has to choose between accuracy and speed. cuBLAS breaks each double-precision number into integer pieces, multiplies them on the GPU’s Tensor Cores, and reassembles the exact result. The answers keep full double-precision accuracy, but the work runs on faster hardware.
Two new algorithms make this more efficient:
Ozaki-II
needs fewer integer multiplications than the earlier
Ozaki-I
approach, and the
2M method
cuts a complex matrix multiplication from four real multiplications to two. This builds on the
Automatic Dynamic Precision (ADP) framework
introduced in
Unlocking Tensor Core Performance with Floating Point Emulation in cuBLAS
, which delivers higher double-precision (FP64) matrix-multiplication performance by mapping FP64 arithmetic onto integer Tensor Cores while preserving native FP64 accuracy.
cuBLAS delivers automatic acceleration of DGEMM and ZGEMM with no application code changes. Because speed matters only when accuracy is not compromised, we validate both on real-world applications: coupled cluster singles and doubles (CCSD) in quantum chemistry, and BerkeleyGW in materials science. This post explains how the algorithms work, shows benchmark and application results, and covers how to get started.
Performance highlights
cuBLAS in CUDA Toolkit 13.4.2 delivers the following performance gains:
cuBLAS DGEMM with Ozaki-II runs 5.5x and 3.9x faster than native FP64 on NVIDIA VR NVL72 and NVIDIA GB200, respectively. It’s also 2x faster than Ozaki-I on NVIDIA GB200.
CCSD case study using cuBLAS DGEMM with Ozaki-II achieves 2x and 1.4x end-to-end speedup over native FP64 on NVIDIA VR NVL72 and NVIDIA GB200 in FP64. In domain-specific mixed-precision mode, end-to-end speedup over native FP64 is 5x and 3.5x on NVIDIA VR NVL72 and NVIDIA GB200 respectively.
cuBLAS ZGEMM with 2M algorithm achieves a 5x speedup over native Complex FP64 (CFP64) on NVIDIA GB200.
BerkeleyGW case study using cuBLAS ZGEMM with 2M algorithm achieves 6.6x and 3.9x speedup over native ZGEMM on NVIDIA VR NVL72 and NVIDIA GB200 respectively.
cuBLAS DGEMM with Ozaki-II achieves up to 175, 147, and 37 TFLOPS on NVIDIA VR NVL72, NVIDIA GB200, NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 respectively.
From Ozaki-I to Ozaki-II
Ozaki-I and Ozaki-II schemes share a common first step, but differ in how the big integer multiplication is performed. Both the schemes align the exponents of the input matrices and convert them to a shared-exponent, variable-length integer representation so that products accumulate exactly on integer Tensor Cores. cuBLAS uses heuristics to automatically choose between Ozaki-I and Ozaki-II for best performance. The integer width is chosen by ADP at runtime or can also be set explicitly by the user.
Ozaki-I
breaks each big integer into 8-bit slices and multiplies slices of A against slices of B in a triangular pattern, so the number of Tensor Core GEMMs grows with the
square
of the slice count.
Ozaki-II
uses a faster big-integer multiplication algorithm based on the Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT). It reduces each quantized operand modulo a set of small pairwise-coprime integers, performs exactly
one
integer GEMM per modulus, and reconstructs the exact product from the residues. With Ozaki-II, the GEMM count is linear in the number of moduli, whereas Ozaki-I grows with the square of the slice count, so the advantage widens as the accuracy target rises. At the accuracy required to match FP64, Ozaki-I needs roughly twice as many Tensor Core GEMMs as Ozaki-II.
Because Ozaki-II materializes one residue pair per modulus, a naive implementation would carry a much larger workspace than Ozaki-I. However, cuBLAS already applies the memory-parsimonious tiling introduced for Ozaki-I in CTK 13.3 to Ozaki-II scheme as well, discarding each residue pair immediately after its GEMM. This results in a more manageable workspace size.
cuBLAS ADP framework is designed to provide accuracy guarantees comparable to, or better than, standard floating-point GEMM algorithms. More information on the accuracy of fixed-point methods can be found in the references. If at run-time, the number of mantissa bits required to preserve FP64-equivalent accuracy exceeds the library default or a user-supplied maximum, cuBLAS falls-back to a code path that utilizes the native FP64 MMA instructions. So, applications can safely use cuBLAS in their production deployments without worrying about numerical accuracy. Figure 1, below, shows the speedup of cuBLAS DGEMM using Ozaki-II over Ozaki-I on GB200.
DGEMM performance
Figure 1. Speedup of DGEMM with Ozaki-II scheme in cuBLAS shipped with CTK 13.4.2 over the Ozaki-I scheme in CTK 13.3.1 on GB200
NVIDIA Rubin
Rubin introduces a new numeric format, TI16 (12-bit integer in sign-magnitude format with range of [-2047, +2047]), that is aptly suited for the acceleration of Ozaki scheme computations. cuBLAS 13.4 uses TI16 type for acceleration of Ozaki-I and Ozaki-II computations through the
tcgen05.mma
instruction on NVIDIA Rubin GPUs (compute capability 10.7). Figure 2, below, shows the speedup of cuBLAS DGEMM using Ozaki-II over native FP64 on VR NVL72.
Figure 2. Speedup of DGEMM with Ozaki-II scheme over native FP64 on VR NVL72
DGEMM application performance – CCSD in quantum chemistry
To demonstrate the potential application performance of Ozaki-II DGEMM, we consider the use case of coupled cluster singles and doubles (CCSD). CCSD is a foundational post-DFT method in electronic structure that together with the (T) perturbative correction (not considered here) forms the “gold standard” of quantum chemistry.
Moreover, the response of CCSD to various perturbations yields the EOM-CCSD treatment of electronic excited states and the CCSD lambda treatment of property computations. CCSD is noteworthy for its very high cost of dense FP64 tensor contractions, which the Ozaki-II scheme in cuBLAS can significantly accelerate.
A small CCSD demonstration was implemented using cuBLAS in CTK 13.4.2 for the main tensor contractions, with the coupled cluster problem setup accelerated by cuEST v0.2.2. A standard FP64 single-GPU T1-transformed restricted CCSD approach was constructed in the density fitting representation. Figure 3, below, shows performance data for frozen-core CCSD/cc-pVTZ for five mid-sized members of the S22 database — these systems contain 24–28 atoms and roughly 590–630 atomic orbitals.
Ozaki-II DGEMM with ESC guaranteeing full FP64 precision causes performance to rise monotonically with generation, yielding a total speedup of 4.7x of Rubin over A100. Another compelling possibility is to use an application-specific mixed precision mode with a fixed Ozaki-II mantissa bit budget, here selected to be 32 mantissa bits. This also yields monotonic performance gains, with total speedup now at 11.5x native FP64 A100. With ESC at full FP64 quality, results are indistinguishable from native FP64 precision – errors in the CCSD correlation energy are <10
-14
E
h
.
Ozaki-II emulation provides the opportunity to use lower fixed precision with 32 mantissa bits while still providing sufficient accuracy for the vast majority of practical applications; errors in the energy are <10
-10
E
h
and the amplitude equations can be converged to a residual of 10
-9
or better.
On Rubin for uracil dimer frozen-core CCSD/cc-pVTZ, fixed precision with 32 mantissa bits achieves an end-to-end throughput of 173 TFLOPS; the throughput of individual GEMMs is as high as 368 TFLOPS with an average GEMM throughput of 200 TFLOPS. Similar throughputs are obtained during the solution of the CCSD lambda response equations needed for molecular property calculations (not shown in plot).
Figure 3. End-to-end speedup of CCSD/cc-pVTZ calculations across GPU generations. Speedups are calculated from the total time to complete CCSD calculations on five different nonbonded complexes. *A new ESC algorithm is used in this performance measurement
Complex GEMMs: from 4M to 3M to 2M
A complex GEMM is conventionally computed as four real GEMMs (4M) of the same size:
A = Ar + i(Ai); B = Br + i(Bi)
C = A x B = (Ar·Br − Ai·Bi) + i(Ar·Bi + Ai·Br)
The well-known 3M algorithm reduces this to three real GEMMs plus quadratic-time pre- and post-processing. In floating-point arithmetic, 3M is used cautiously because forming the sums Ar + Ai and Br + Bi, and subtracting the intermediate products during reconstruction can degrade numerical stability.
With the Ozaki-II scheme, the additions, subtractions, and products are all exact integer operations, so the choice of complex multiplication method no longer affects the accuracy of the result. Multiplying two complex numbers cannot be done in fewer than three real multiplications, but matrix products in this exact integer setting are not bound by that result: the 2M algorithm computes a complex product with only two real GEMMs instead of four. The end result is that a ZGEMM now costs roughly twice a real GEMM of the same size instead of four times. The full derivation is available in the
2M paper
.
Starting with CUDA Toolkit 13.4, cuBLAS uses the 2M algorithm to accelerate ZGEMM and Figure-4 shows the speedup achieved by the 2M + Ozaki-II scheme over the traditional 4M method on GB200.
Figure 4. Speed-up of ZGEMM with 2M + Ozaki-II scheme in CTK 13.4.1 over native 4M method on GB20
ZGEMM application performance – BerkeleyGW
The
BerkeleyGW
code is used by researchers to study physical properties of materials that emerge as a result of how electrons change energy states. It is a massively parallel code that has been used at full scale on leadership class supercomputers. Using GPUs with BerkeleyGW can lead to an 86x performance speedup over the CPU-only implementation and can be even further accelerated with the latest cuBLAS enhancements to ZGEMM.
By default, cuBLAS uses its ADP framework to determine the parameters that will provide accuracy guarantees comparable to, or better than, standard complex floating-point (CFP64) GEMM algorithm in the CHISUM routine of the BerkeleyGW
Epsilon module
. This is done automatically for users without any application code changes. We evaluated accuracy and performance in the following configurations: Native ZGEMM, Ozaki-II 2M with ADP and Ozaki-II 2M with 53 bits, which all produced the same Epsilon matrix elements for up to 10 decimal places as specified in the
NERSC-10 harness
.
On GB200, moving from native ZGEMM to Ozaki-II 2M with 53 bits delivers a 3.9x end-to-end speedup. Similarly, we observe a 6.6x speedup on VR NVL72. Overall, we observe a 5.8x speedup going from native ZGEMM on Blackwell to ZGEMM using Ozaki-II 2M with 53 bits on VR NVL72. Figure-5 shows the end-to-end performance speedup running the Epsilon module of BerkeleyGW with a reference problem size (Si998) on 32 Blackwell and Rubin GPUs (2 Grace CPUs + 4 B200 GPUs per node and 2 Vera CPUs + 4 R100 GPUs per node).
Figure 5. End-to-end speedup of the BerkeleyGW Epsilon module on the Si998 reference problem, comparing native ZGEMM against Ozaki-II 2M with ADP and with a 53-bit mantissa budget. Measured on 32 GPUs: GB200 – 2 Grace CPUs + 4 B200 GPUs per node and Vera Rubin – 2 Vera CPUs + 4 R100 GPUs per node
DGEMM performance on GB200, RTX PRO 6000
Figure 6, below, shows the speedup of DGEMM with Ozaki-II over native FP64 on GB200. At the smallest shapes, ADP has determined that the Ozaki-II path offers no advantage and dispatched to native FP64, but the performance gains grows steadily with larger M, N and K values reaching 3.9x at the largest shapes measured.
Figure 6. Speedup of DGEMM with Ozaki-II scheme over native FP64 on GB200
The upper-bound of the performance gain depends on how much integer Tensor Core throughput a GPU has relative to its native FP64 units, and that ratio varies widely across the product line with NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition at the far end of that range. Figure 7, below, shows the speedup of DGEMM with Ozaki-II over native FP64 on RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell SE. As can be observed from the figure, Ozaki-II benefits the full spectrum of matrix sizes tested, with even the smallest gaining 10x over native FP64 and the largest reaching 23x.
Figure 7. Speedup of DGEMM with Ozaki-II scheme over native FP64 on RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell SE
Getting started
Download and install the latest
NVIDIA CUDA Toolkit
Read the
floating point emulation section of the cuBLAS documentation
for full API details, including cublasSetEmulationStrategy() and manual mantissa bit control.
Explore the
cuBLAS Emulation samples on GitHub
Evaluate the gains on your own workloads and tell us what you find, we want feedback on both the API design and the precision/performance trade-off. You can reach us on the
NVIDIA Accelerated Computing Developer Forum

AI-Generated Summary
NVIDIA cuPhoton
.xBeam accelerates radio interferometry correlation for the Event Horizon Telescope by processing voltage recordings into visibilities on GPUs.
The FX correlator ingests VDIF frames, applies delay and fringe corrections, channelizes signals via FFT, cross-multiplies station pairs, and writes visibilities in DiFX SWIN or xbeam-v1 format.
On an NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 system with 64 GPUs and GPUDirect Storage, xBeam correlated a 10 TB dataset in 70 seconds, achieving a 460x speedup over an x86 CPU baseline of 31,992 seconds.
Scaling splits observation time across GPUs using --devices on a single node or --shard-count and --shard-index across nodes, with merge-shards combining partial SWIN outputs into a complete visibility set.
AI agents can orchestrate end-to-end pipelines by parsing VDIF metadata, generating JSON job specifications, launching xBeam correlation across GPU clusters, and monitoring execution.
Next Steps
Explore the
NVIDIA cuPhoton repository
for imaging modules, xBeam, and sample recordings with job files.
Read the
Faster Scientific Image Analysis with NVIDIA cuPhoton
walkthrough for an imaging-focused tutorial.
Review the
NVIDIA cuPhoton product page
for additional resources and related examples.
Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.
Learn more
Imaging black holes is challenging because they are distant and appear tiny in the sky—for example, M87*’s observed ring spans just 42 microarcseconds. The black hole itself emits no light, so telescopes capture radio emission from superheated gas swirling outside the event horizon. The black hole’s intense gravity bends the paths of this light, shaping the bright ring that frames the central shadow.
The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) addresses this challenge by linking 13 radio observatory stations across locations, including Hawaii, Chile, Spain, Mexico, and the South Pole, through very-long-baseline interferometry (VLBI). These stations record millimeter and submillimeter radio signals as high-speed voltage streams, which are synchronized and combined to reconstruct detailed images. The next-generation EHT (ngEHT) aims to add observing sites to improve image quality and track changes around black holes over time.
This post walks through GPU-based interferometry with cuPhoton.xBeam, from reading telescope recordings to generating visibilities and scaling across multiple GPUs. These measurements serve as inputs to downstream calibration and image reconstruction, which are outside the scope of this tutorial.
Figure 1. Radio telescopes record signals that are correlated into visibilities for image reconstruction. Conceptual illustration
NVIDIA cuPhoton
.xBeam performs GPU-based correlation for interferometry and organizes recorded data for parallel reads. It correlates signals from pairs of telescopes to produce one complex visibility for each pair of stations, each frequency channel, and each short time interval. The next step can involve constructing a 3D gas model from these visibilities via a distinct downstream process, such as Gaussian splatting. This method models the emitting gas as numerous compact, glowing blobs moving along orbits near a spinning black hole, optimized to match the observed visibilities. cuPhoton does not currently incorporate this second component.
The NVIDIA cuPhoton team collaborates with the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics and the MIT Haystack Observatory to accelerate data ingestion and correlation using xBeam. Running on an NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 system with 64 GPUs and GPUDirect Storage (GDS) in compatibility mode, xBeam processed a 10 TB dataset in
70 seconds
—about
460x faster than
an x86 CPU baseline of 31,992 seconds (8.89 hours).
The sky is an inverse problem
The EHT records radio signals in two polarizations at up to 64 gigabits per second per telescope, generating petabytes of data. Correlating signals between telescope pairs produces visibilities, which sample Fourier components of the sky’s brightness. Earth’s rotation traces sparse measurement tracks, and reconstruction algorithms combine these samples into an image. Rapid changes in sources such as Sgr A* complicate this process because observations capture an evolving source over time.
An Earth-sized array observing at 1.3 mm only collects (u, v) measurements along the elliptical tracks drawn by Earth’s rotation. Because no physical lens forms the image directly, reconstructive algorithms must solve an inverse problem to synthesize the picture from sparse samples. For targets like Sgr A*, the source changes during an observation session, complicating reconstruction methods that assume a static source (
Focus on First Sgr A* Results
).
Figure 2 shows the imaging workflow using a synthetic source. The left panel shows the (u, v) tracks that an array laid out like the 2017 EHT samples over one night as Earth turns. The next panel shows visibility amplitudes, |V(u, v)| plotted against baseline length, followed by a dirty image formed from the sparse samples. The right panel shows a crescent model, a simple ring-shaped image that researchers can fit to those amplitudes.
Figure 2. Synthetic EHT-like example showing spatial-frequency sampling, visibility amplitudes, a dirty image, and a crescent model
Light passing near a black hole can orbit it before escaping, forming a thin photon ring near the shadow’s edge. Its size and shape can help constrain the black hole’s mass, spin, and viewing angle, while its interferometric signal produces characteristic oscillations. The proposed Black Hole Explorer (BHEX) aims to measure this ring, and future ngEHT observations at 345 GHz could detect its signature through polarization measurements.
What cuPhoton.xBeam computes
cuPhoton.xBeam is the FX correlator in the cuPhoton toolkit. It restructures the recordings so they can be read in parallel, builds a .vdix index so later reads jump straight to each frame, and loads the voltages into GPU memory. Then it does the FX work, like DiFX (CPU-based, open-source software correlator): it Fourier-transforms each station’s voltage into frequency channels (F) and cross-multiplies the station and polarization pairs at each frequency channel requested by the job (X). Those steps run on the GPU. In order, xBeam does five things:
1. Ingest
. Read the VDIF frames and place each one at its correct time. xBeam builds a small index file, the
.vdix
sidecar, that records where every frame is without copying the data, so later reads jump straight to the right place.
xBeam indexes VDIF frames by timestamp, thread, and physical location. Its .vdix sidecars let subsequent reads locate the required data without rewriting the recording. Missing or invalid data remain explicitly tracked.
2. Delay and fringe
. Shift each station’s samples by the delay in the job’s model, so the same wavefront lines up at every station, and remove the phase drift caused by Earth’s motion. Delay correction spans both sides of the fast Fourier transform (FFT). Integer-sample alignment and fringe rotation occur before channelization; a frequency-dependent phase correction handles the remaining fractional-sample delay afterward.
3. Channelize.
Run an FFT on each station’s voltage stream to split it into frequency channels.
4. Cross-multiply and accumulate
. For every pair of stations, multiply each channel’s spectrum from one station by the complex conjugate of the corresponding spectrum from the other station and sum the products over the integration time. Invalid input is masked, and the accumulated products are normalized using validity-derived exposure weights. The selected processing profile controls additional admission and reported-weight conventions.
5. Write visibilities
. Save the result in DiFX’s SWIN format or in xBeam’s own
xbeam-v1
format, whichever the job asks for.
The delay xBeam applies comes from the job file. It is a sum of different delays: the geometric delay, which is parameterized as a polynomial in time around a reference time

. The phase correction applied to the samples is

where

xBeam does not compute delays from station positions. It uses the delays given in the job. It also does not trace light paths around a black hole. DiFX is the CPU correlator used as the reference for validating xBeam results. Tools such as HOPS, rPICARD, and
eht-imaging
take the visibilities from there for calibration and imaging.
Data moves from disk into GPU memory in one of two ways: standard POSIX reads through pinned host memory, or reads through cuFile, the GPUDirect Storage API. Whether cuFile uses a direct storage-to-GPU path depends on the configuration and runtime conditions. The phase correction, the FFT, and the cross-multiply all run on the GPU. Jobs that use several GPUs split the scan in time (
--shard-count
,
--shard-index
), and
merge-shards
joins the partial SWIN outputs.
Figure 3. cuPhoton.xBeam processes telescope recordings into visibilities for downstream imaging
Run one job
xBeam (part of cuPhoton v0.1.3) takes a normalized JSON job, schema version 1, or a supported DiFX .input file. A sample recording and matching job file can be found in the
NVIDIA/cuPhoton
repository. The job names stations, clocks, frequencies, VDIF datastreams, baselines, and scans. Point JOB.json at the recordings. The output directory must be new. The run writes visibilities in the job’s output format, swin or xbeam-v1. Readers can verify a successful run by checking that the output matches the expected SWIN visibility records and validating the completion headers.
Inspect a recording first. inspect-vdif reads headers only:
cuphoton xbeam inspect-vdif RECORDING.vdif --json
VDIF files may contain interleaved threads, missing frames, or frames stored out of timestamp order. Build .vdix sidecars before correlation so xBeam can locate the requested timestamp ranges without rewriting the recordings. Reuse them while the source files remain unchanged. Every later read then jumps straight to the right frame. The builder uses cuFile by default; pass
--backend posix
if the machine does not have GPUDirect Storage:
cuphoton xbeam build-vdif-sidecar RECORDING-*.vdif \
--index-dir SIDECARS \
--backend cufile \
--devices 0,1,2,3
Run the correlation on the GPU. –backend cupy selects the GPU path. By default, xBeam reads data through pinned host memory (POSIX). –vdif-io cufile selects the cuFile I/O path through GPUDirect Storage. That is the mode used in the Vera Rubin runs, and it needs no other flags.
cuphoton xbeam correlate JOB.json \
--output RUN \
--backend cupy \
--vdif-io cufile \
--scan SCAN_ID \
--first-integration 0 \
--integration-count N \
--index-dir SIDECARS
The same job can run from Python.
load_job
returns the same job object the command line uses.
correlate
returns visibility records one at a time; writing SWIN files is left to the command-line tool.
from cuphoton.xbeam import CorrelationWindow, correlate, load_job
job = load_job("JOB.json")
window = CorrelationWindow("SCAN_ID", first_integration=0, integration_count=8)
for record in correlate(
job,
backend="cupy",
window=window,
index_dir="SIDECARS",
vdif_io="cufile",
):
spectrum = record.spectrum  # complex visibilities for one baseline product
Gaps in a recording affect how the correlator assigns times and weights to subsequent samples. xBeam offers an explicit buffered-reader policy through
--profile interop-real-usb-buffered-window-replay-v1
.
Within a retained reader buffer, this policy continues consuming recorded samples using the buffer’s existing time reference until the next allocation establishes a new anchor. It also determines which FFT blocks contribute and their reported visibility weights.
It does not recover missing samples, and a full reported weight does not mean every timestamp was recorded. Without replay, xBeam aligns subsequent frames by their header timestamps and marks missing slots invalid, which can produce different visibilities and weights.

items.title: Catch Go bugs that fuzzing misses with Gemini and a constraint solver How pairing Go's surviving compiler bounds-check traps with Gemini 4 Argon and the Z3 constraint solver catche
items.content:
Catch Go bugs that fuzzing misses with Gemini and a constraint solver
- Google Developers Blog
Catch Go bugs that fuzzing misses with Gemini and a constraint solver
NOV. 12, 2026
Karl Weinmeister
Director, Developer Relations
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
I help lead Google's
agent skills program
, currently with 175 agent skills that supplement community collections like
go-skills
. To keep that many skill files consistent, I wrote skill-lint, a standalone
Go
CLI that checks SKILL.md files and applies LLM-generated line edits before they ship. Even with skill-lint's own unit and fuzz test suite, a small slice or line-number mistake inside its Markdown parsers or edit applier can sit dormant until an unusual file or edit range triggers a runtime panic in the linter.
In Go, every slice or index operation that can panic at runtime compiles down to an explicit bounds-check trap in machine code, after the compiler's optimizer strips out the checks it can already rule out. To hunt for crashes, I compiled key functions from my code to see which panic traps survived optimization, and
Gemini 4 Argon
translated the path to each trap into rules for the
Z3 constraint solver
. An LLM-written solver model isn't a sound proof system, but it gives the agent an independent way to reason about control flow and synthesize concrete Go reproducers, and every crash it finds is real because go test runs the offending bytes directly. That workflow caught all three bugs I planted in test parsers and turned up three latent bugs in skill-lint.
In this post, I'll walk through how the Gemini and Z3 pipeline works, why
go test -fuzz
missed two of those crashes (and the one-line change that fixes it), and where this approach fits in a day-to-day Go workflow.
How the solver pipeline works
A
recent post from Anthropic
showed how formal verification catches latent bugs in C and C++ by having frontier AI models write machine-checked
Rocq
proofs across
OSS-Fuzz
libraries. Instead of sampling random inputs like a fuzzer, a formal tool works backward from each failure condition to solve for the exact input that triggers it. Full theorem proving is still too heavy for most day-to-day Go projects, so I wanted to see how much of that bug-hunting power an agent can get from an LLM and a constraint solver in about a minute per function.
In C and C++, reading or writing past the end of a buffer corrupts memory. Go catches out-of-bounds access at runtime instead, compiling every slice or index operation it can't prove safe into an explicit branch to
runtime.panicBounds
that panics, crashing the process unless recovered.
Before generating machine code, Go's
SSA
prove
pass already eliminates most of those checks by tracking slice lengths and loop variables. That optimization pass leaves behind only the
runtime.panicBounds
traps the compiler couldn't rule out on its own, giving the solver a short list of candidate crash sites to target.
I compiled each target with
GOOS=linux GOARCH=riscv64 go build -gcflags="-S -d=ssa/check_bce/debug=1"
(
-S
prints the assembly listing and
ssa/check_bce/debug=1
logs every surviving bounds check) and passed both the Go source and the disassembly to the model. Looking at Go source alone, you can't see which bounds checks the compiler already removed or where a register gets truncated to 8 bits; in the disassembly, both show up. I targeted
RISC-V
because it's the instruction set Anthropic's post targets for its Rocq proofs, and Go cross-compiles to it out of the box.
From there, Argon read the Go source and disassembly and returned a Z3 script modeling the path to each surviving trap, along with a patched function whenever it flagged a bug. Z3 then checked whether those constraints could be satisfied, and whenever it found a crashing input,
go test
replayed those bytes against the real function. Using an LLM saved me from translating assembly into solver constraints by hand. Argon's translation dominated the runtime, at about a minute per function, while Z3 itself finished in milliseconds.
Go's SSA compiler strips out provably safe bounds checks first. Gemini 4 Argon then models the remaining traps for Z3 to check.
When to trust the solver
Anthropic's approach relies on
interactive theorem proving
, where experts model machine semantics and Rocq checks LLM-generated proofs against those rules. In contrast, my workflow uses a constraint solver based on
satisfiability modulo theories (SMT)
, relying on Argon to translate assembly directly into Z3 constraints. While a constraint solver doesn't provide a complete correctness proof without a semantic model, it is highly effective for finding bugs. Z3's
check-sat
command returns sat when input constraints can be satisfied and
unsat
when they cannot.
A sat answer ("definitely buggy") comes with concrete bytes aimed at the trap, and
go test
runs them against the real function. Once go test panics, you have a concrete bug reproducer regardless of whether Argon's model was sound. Like a Bloom filter for bugs, an
unsat
answer only means "maybe correct." Trading away a correctness proof is what makes the approach so practical: you get most of the bug-finding value of formal methods for a tiny fraction of the effort.
Anthropic's setup proved no-crash properties on whole binaries under a 64 MB budget; I checked individual functions on fresh 64-byte slices where
cap(buf) == len(buf)
, so any slice past
len(buf)
panics. (If you want the full-binary Rocq setup for Go,
theorem-labs/oss-verify
includes a
Go 1.27
runtime overlay that makes the runtime single-threaded and deterministic.)
For the fuzzing baseline, I ran unseeded
go test -fuzz
on Go 1.27.3 against each planted bug: one 3-second run and three 60-second runs, each with a fresh fuzz cache so a short time budget wouldn't explain a miss.
Finding a planted bug in assembly
I started with three safe parsers to make sure the pipeline didn't flag clean code. The compiler's
prove
pass removed every bounds check in a TOML key parser on its own, and Z3 returned
unsat
on the remaining traps in an HTTP header scanner and a varint decoder.
Then I wrote three parsers with subtle panics. Here's the first one,
ParseTwoChunkFrame
:
func ParseTwoChunkFrame(buf []byte) ([]byte, []byte) {
if len(buf) < 4 || buf[0] != 0xA5 || buf[1] != 0x5A {
return nil, nil
}
hdrLen, bodyLen := buf[2], buf[3]
total := hdrLen + bodyLen
if int(total)+4 > len(buf) {
return nil, nil
}
endHdr := 4 + int(hdrLen)
endBody := endHdr + int(bodyLen)
return buf[4:endHdr], buf[endHdr:endBody]
}
Go
Copied
In the RISC-V disassembly, the bug is much easier to see:
0x0060  ADD    X16, X9, X5                 ; X5 = hdrLen + bodyLen
0x0064  MOVBU  X5, X5                      ; TRUNCATE to uint8: X5 = X5 & 0xff
0x0068  ADDI   $4, X5, X5                  ; X5 = int(total) + 4
0x006a  BLT    X11, X5, 0x00bc             ; guard: if len(buf) < X5, return nil, nil
0x006e  MOV    X9, X11                     ; X11 = int(hdrLen)
0x0070  MOV    X16, X14                    ; X14 = int(bodyLen)
0x0072  ADD    X14, X11, X9                ; X9 = int(hdrLen) + int(bodyLen) (unmasked!)
0x0076  ADDI   $4, X11, X16                ; X16 = endHdr = 4 + int(hdrLen)
0x007a  BLTU   X12, X16, 0x00ec            ; if cap(buf) < endHdr -> runtime.panicBounds
...
0x0090  ADDI   $4, X9, X9                  ; X9 = endBody = 4 + int(hdrLen) + int(bodyLen)
0x0092  BLTU   X12, X9, 0x00e8             ; if cap(buf) < endBody -> runtime.panicBounds
Plain text
Copied
total := hdrLen + bodyLen
adds two
uint8
values, so
MOVBU
wraps the sum at 256
before the length guard checks it, while
endBody
adds the full 64-bit ints. Argon turned those instructions into a Z3 query asking whether a fresh slice of up to 64 bytes can pass the guard and still fail the
endBody
check at
0x0092
:
import z3
s = z3.Solver()
length, capacity = z3.BitVecs("length capacity", 64)
b0, b1, hdrLen8, bodyLen8 = z3.BitVecs("b0 b1 hdrLen8 bodyLen8", 8)
wrapped_sum64 = z3.ZeroExt(56, hdrLen8 + bodyLen8) + z3.BitVecVal(4, 64)
end_hdr64 = z3.BitVecVal(4, 64) + z3.ZeroExt(56, hdrLen8)
end_body64 = end_hdr64 + z3.ZeroExt(56, bodyLen8)
s.add(z3.UGE(length, 4), z3.ULE(length, 64), capacity == length)
s.add(b0 == 0xA5, b1 == 0x5A)
s.add(z3.UGE(length, wrapped_sum64), z3.ULE(end_hdr64, capacity))
s.add(z3.UGT(end_body64, capacity))  # panic at 0x0092
assert s.check() == z3.sat
print(s.model())
Python
Copied
Z3 returned a 59-byte counterexample with
hdrLen = 48
and
bodyLen = 236
: their
uint8
sum wraps from 284 down to 28 (so 28 + 4 ≤ 59 passes the guard), and
buf[endHdr:endBody]
then slices to index 288 and panics.
Why Go's fuzzer missed a 1-in-5 crash
At 59 bytes, 19.4% of all possible
(hdrLen, bodyLen)
pairs trigger this crash. Yet a 3-second fuzz run missed it, and so did three 60-second runs.
Go checks a
slice expression
like
buf[endHdr:endBody]
against the slice's capacity, not its length, and Go's fuzzer rarely passes a slice without spare capacity. In a 10-second probe of 386,741 fuzz calls, 89% of inputs were views into a shared ~100 MB buffer, and only 0.07% had
cap == len
. With that much spare capacity, endBody (at most 514) never exceeds
cap(buf)
, so the buggy parser returns bytes past the end of
buf
instead of panicking.
The second target,
ExtractQuotedToken
, hit the same blind spot when a trailing backslash pushed the index one byte past
len(buf)
. Z3 caught it immediately with the 2-byte input
[]byte{'"', '\\'}
, while the fuzzer absorbed the overrun in spare capacity.
Clipping capacity to length with a full slice expression turns any slice past
len
into a panic:
f.Fuzz(func(t *testing.T, data []byte) {
data = data[:len(data):len(data)] // cap == len: slicing past the end now panics
ParseTwoChunkFrame(data)
})
Go
Copied
After that change, the fuzzer crashed both
ParseTwoChunkFrame
and
ExtractQuotedToken
in all three runs (median 0.28 s and 0.17 s). The third target,
ParseMagicPacket
, was a control because its signed
int8
length bug panics on a negative index regardless of capacity, and the fuzzer found it in every run either way. Fuzzing still can't give you an
unsat
signal across the remaining paths, which is how I checked the three safe parsers and Argon's patches.
Clipping slice capacity to length fixes the fuzzer's blind spot on both overrun bugs, while Argon and Z3 catch all three crashes and check each patched parser.
Running it on skill-lint
Next, I pointed the pipeline at skill-lint itself. A whole Go CLI is too large to hand to a solver directly. Even a 10-line parser links 1,559 symbols from the Go runtime, and the 28 MB skill-lint binary has 32,321 symbols in total. Following
Functional Core, Imperative Shell
, I left CLI flags, network calls, and file I/O to
go test -fuzz
and
go test -race
, and ran the solver only on pure functions and slice helpers extracted from file-reading code.
Pull parsing and slice math into pure functions for the solver, and leave file I/O, CLI flags, and network calls to standard fuzzing and race detection.
Of the five functions I tested, two scanners came back
unsat
(including a CRLF line splitter with six surviving bounds checks), and the other three had bugs. The sharpest was in
ApplyReplacementChunks
, which validates LLM-generated
{StartLine, EndLine}
edits against the initial line count and sorts them bottom-to-top so earlier edits don't shift later line numbers:
for _, c := range chunks {
if c.StartLine < 1 || c.EndLine > len(lines) || c.StartLine > c.EndLine {

items.content:
How Agent Anomaly Detection scores on benchmarks we didn't write
- Google Developers Blog
How Agent Anomaly Detection scores on benchmarks we didn't write
NOV. 12, 2026
Nakul Javali
Senior Software Engineer
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
AI agents now read email, book travel and move money for the people who use them. Every tool call also pulls in text that someone else wrote, and whoever controls that text can try to steer the agent. OWASP calls this agent goal hijack and ranks it first in its
Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026)
.
Figure 1: An indirect prompt injection. The harmful instruction arrives inside data that a tool returns, not from the user.
In September we
announced
Agent Anomaly Detection in Private Preview on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. It reads your agents' traces and logs asynchronously, without adding latency, and flags sessions where an agent acts outside its intended boundaries. We tested this feature against benchmarks for this top risk of agent goal hijack.
Security tools tend to look good on tests their own team wrote, so we ran five non-Google-written, public agent-security benchmarks through Agent Anomaly Detection without changing anything. In four of them, the harmful instruction hides in data that a tool returns. In the fifth, the user asks for harm directly.
The model itself didn't follow about half of the harmful instructions it read. It refused three in four direct requests for harm, and ignored or failed at about 30% of the instructions hidden in tool output. Of the ones that were executed, Agent Anomaly Detection flagged 87% for post-execution review. It raised false alarms on 2% to 16% of benign sessions, depending on the tools the agent uses. Poisoned memory is the clear gap: when instructions planted in the agent’s long-term memory made it act, Agent Anomaly Detection caught 4 of 18.
How we ran the test
Figure 2: The test setup. Agent Anomaly Detection and the benchmark's check see the same agent run, but only the check reads the final state of the apps.
We ran each benchmark case through an agent built with the Agent Development Kit (ADK) using
gemini-2.5-flash
, on the benchmark's simulated apps. The agent sent its traces and logs to Agent Anomaly Detection, as a customer's agent would. Then the benchmark's own Python check read the final state of the apps, such as whether money left the account, and labeled the session. Deterministic code decides the label, not a model, so an injected instruction can't mislead the grader, and Agent Anomaly Detection cannot cheat the benchmark. Each agent first ran at least 300 benign sessions, because Agent Anomaly Detection learns how each agent usually behaves.
We also recorded whether a tool returned the harmful instruction to the agent. In many cases, the agent never opens the email or file that holds it. So each harmful session ends one of three ways:
Never read
: no tool returned the instruction, so the agent never saw it.
Resisted
: the agent read the instruction but didn't follow it. This includes an agent that tried and failed.
Carried out
: the agent read the instruction and followed it. The benchmark's own check decides this.
In AgentHarm, the user sends the request, so the agent always reads it.
The five benchmarks are
AgentDojo
(NeurIPS 2024),
InjecAgent
(ACL 2024 Findings),
Agent Security Bench
(ASB, ICLR 2025),
AgentDyn
(2026) and
AgentHarm
(ICLR 2025). ASB plants the instruction in the agent's long-term memory. In all, Agent Anomaly Detection scored 1,774 sessions.
What we found
Agent Anomaly Detection flagged 87% of the harmful instructions that the agent carried out, and raised a few false alarms on ordinary office work. It's strongest on goal hijack and tool misuse, and weakest on poisoned memory.
Results by OWASP category
Each finding carries a threat category, and four of Agent Anomaly Detection’s five categories align with the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications. We graded each OWASP category on what this study showed, not on what Agent Anomaly Detection is designed to catch.
Public benchmarks concentrate on goal hijack and tool misuse, so our evidence is strongest there. We did not find public benchmarks with labeled agent traces for cascading failures or for identity and privilege abuse. Shared benchmarks for those categories would help the whole field.
Agent Anomaly Detection flags most of what gets past the model
Figure 3: What happened to each harmful session, on the four benchmarks with an outcome split.
By benchmark, Agent Anomaly Detection flagged 85% of the carried-out harmful instructions on AgentDojo, 87% on InjecAgent, 99% on AgentDyn and 81% on AgentHarm. Over all harmful sessions, including the ones that the agent never read or resisted, it flagged 45% to 62%. In the 141 sessions where the agent never read the instruction, nothing happened, and it flagged just 1.
Figure 4: For each app, the share of harmful instructions that the agent carried out and that Agent Anomaly Detection flagged. The counts in some apps are small.
Results held across the apps
. In 8 of the 11 apps, Agent Anomaly Detection flagged at least 95% of the carried-out harmful instructions. The lowest rate was in AgentDojo's Slack app, at 63%. Many of those instructions ask for one small action, such as a page visit, which looks like normal browsing.
A refused request still leaves a record
Agent Anomaly Detection also flags many requests that the agent refuses. In AgentHarm, the agent refused most requests and carried out 108 of 412, and Agent Anomaly Detection still flagged 55% of the refused sessions, because the request sits in the user's own message, which it reads. When the agent didn't follow an instruction hidden in tool output, it flagged only 11% to 25%, because the instruction sits deep inside a tool result.
False alarms depend on the agent's everyday tools
False alarms were rare on ordinary office work: on the three injection benchmarks, whose benign sessions are office tasks, Agent Anomaly Detection flagged 2% to 4% of benign sessions. On AgentHarm it flagged 16%. Those benign tasks are twins of the harmful ones, so they post to social media, run terminal commands and download files. High-impact tools in normal use look more like misuse.
Where we're still improving
Agent Anomaly Detection did less well in five areas. It flagged only 11% to 25% of the instructions that the agent resisted, because a resisted instruction changes little in how the agent behaves. It missed more small actions, like single page visits, because they look like normal work. And it raised more false alarms for agents whose everyday work uses high-impact tools. If your agent is one of them, expect more findings at first, and triage them by severity and threat category.
The other two areas are new agents and poisoned memory. Some Agent Anomaly Detection methods need a few hundred sessions of history: on AgentDyn, it flagged 33% of carried-out harmful instructions when each agent had about 220 benign sessions, and 99% with 360. And it caught only 4 of the 18 sessions where poisoned memory made the agent act.
Here's what we're working on:
Report attempts that the agent resisted, at a lower severity, so you can see when someone is probing your agent.
Catch small actions that reach an untrusted destination, such as a single visit to an unknown web page.
Tell normal use of high-impact tools apart from misuse.
Give new agents full coverage sooner.
Detect instructions planted in long-term memory more reliably.
What this means for your agents
Protect your agents with defense in depth.
Use controls that stop harmful actions before they run, and Agent Anomaly Detection to find what gets through.
Send complete telemetry.
Enable ADK tracing and logging, including prompt and response content.
Screen untrusted content.
Check prompts and tool results for prompt injection with a filter such as Model Armor.
Block risky tool calls before they run.
Semantic Governance Policy
, in Preview, checks each proposed tool call against the user's request and your rules, and denies the ones that don't fit. Agent Anomaly Detection then reports what gets past it.
Require approval for high-impact actions.
Ask a person to approve payments, outbound email, data sharing, or other actions that should have a human in the loop.
Limit each agent's tools.
Give each agent only the tools and permissions its task needs.
Review what gets through.
Agent Anomaly Detection doesn’t block actions. It reports anomalous sessions, and its findings also appear in Security Command Center; route the Critical and High ones to your incident team.
Limits of this study
We used one agent model and simulated apps, and the benchmarks' benign tasks are likely simpler than your production traffic, so your false-alarm rate can differ. Agent Anomaly Detection returned no result for about 6% of the sessions we sent; counting those as misses lowers the overall rates by 1 to 2 points.

Agent Anomaly Detection overview
.

items.title: A2UI 1.0: Build delightful, fast, reliable, agentic experiences A2UI 1.0 is an open protocol for generative UI that enables AI agents to render interactive, native screens across w
items.content:
A2UI 1.0: Build delightful, fast, reliable, agentic experiences
- Google Developers Blog
A2UI 1.0: Build delightful, fast, reliable, agentic experiences
NOV. 11, 2026
Vishal Motwani
A2UI PM
Google A2UI Team
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
User interactions with agents today are where computers were in the terminal era: capable, and answering almost everything in text. Users can ask an agent for anything by typing or talking, and what comes back is usually a wall of text, a poor way to compare three products or edit and approve a detailed plan.
Today
,
we're releasing A2UI 1.0, the first stable version of our open protocol for generative UI. It lets AI agents answer with interactive screens, such as a form to confirm or a chart. Developers can use it now with open-source renderer SDKs for the web, Android, and iOS and agent SDKs for Python, TypeScript, and Dart. Companies such as
Atlassian
,
Alation
,
Bloomberg
, and
ByteDance
are already building with it.
With A2UI, the agent describes what to show, and every app draws the UI with its own native components. The application receives A2UI messages and each app renders the content securely and at native speed. Users get the same low latency, high trust, and complete native fidelity whether they reach a company's agent in its own app or in a third-party AI assistant that hosts MCP apps, such as Gemini or Claude.
Why A2UI
Personalized in the moment.
Your agent constructs a UI that adapts to each user's unique needs and preferences.
Native to your brand.
Agents use your design system and nothing else. They place and configure only the components you register.
Fast, reliable, and secure in production.
LLMs compose UI with
A2UI Express
or with “system one” decision models that pick components instead of writing text. A2UI reliably binds to your data and child components on the server, so sensitive values never reach the model, and the app streams in the UI as the agent works.
What developers can build with A2UI
You wake up sick. Getting through the morning takes six apps: book a video visit, move your meetings, tell your team, turn on an out-of-office reply, ask your partner to do school pickup and order soup. Ask a text-only agent instead, and you get a numbered wall of text, then round after round of “which ones?”. A2UI won't handle your sick day, but it gives developers the framework to build an agent that can. That agent could answer with one view of all six apps. Changing your plan is a couple of taps instead of another round of messages, and nothing is sent until you confirm.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
The same sick day three ways. The third app shows the kind of agent interfaces developers can build with A2UI (illustration).
The same agent output works on any screen. Ask an agent to “move dinner with Priya to Friday”, and it can answer with one view that lines up your calendar, open tables from a restaurant booking app and prices from a rideshare app, so the time that works for everyone is obvious. The developer builds that view once with A2UI, and it renders natively on your phone and on your laptop.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
The same request answered in text and with A2UI, then the same view on a laptop (illustration).
In both examples, A2UI is the framework that simplifies building these experiences across platforms. Developers build the agent and choose the platforms it works with. A2UI gives them the protocol the agent uses to describe each view, a way to combine components from different apps in one view, and renderers that draw it natively on the web, Android, and iOS.
New to A2UI? Start with the
A2UI Playground by CopilotKit
or check out
industry examples
.
A2UI Playground by Copilotkit
What's new in 1.0
A stable protocol.
Version 1.0 adds bidirectional function calls, so a flight or reservation picker can check availability on the spot. The protocol also adds support for accessibility and extensions for any additional metadata.
Renderer libraries for major platforms.
Open-source renderers draw A2UI screens with
React
,
Angular
, and
Lit
on the web;
Flutter
on mobile, web, and desktop;
SwiftUI
on iOS and
Jetpack Compose
on Android (currently v0.9.1, and v1.0 coming soon). The web and Flutter renderers also work inside
MCP Apps
, so A2UI screens can appear in AI assistants that support MCP Apps, such as
Claude
and
Gemini
.
Fast, reliable UI generation with A2UI for Agent SDKs.
New SDKs for
TypeScript
and
Dart
along with
Python
, simplify integration with your agent harness or framework by generating skills, translating messages, and correcting errors. Swappable inference formats reduce latency, and in Python,
A2UI Macros
add programmatic component expansion and data binding.
Teams building with A2UI today
Atlassian
Atlassian is bringing A2UI to Jira, where teams can
assign work items to AI agents
. When an agent needs a follow-up from the team to finish a work item, such as a missing detail or a decision, it asks with an interactive card in the work item, and the team answers right there in Jira.
Figure 1. An agent asks the team for a follow-up inside a Jira work item.
Alation
The Alation Intelligence Operating System (AIOS) builds its feeds using A2UI: metric cards, charts, and more. Each chart can show the SQL query and data behind it. Ask Claude for a feed about profitable products, and the feed renders in the conversation using A2UI to render metric cards, charts, and custom components. The same feed with the same information can be viewed directly inside Alation with a nearly identical layout.
“The Alation Intelligence Operating System (AIOS) brings artifacts with data, charts, and insights directly to where teams work with transparency about where each figure comes from. A2UI provides the interactive UI scaffolding that makes these artifacts feel like high-touch, tailored applications, whether they are used in Alation or in the AI Assistants our customers already use.”
-
GT Volpe, Vice President of Product Management at Alation
Figure 2. The same Alation feed rendered in Claude (left) and in Alation's Data Products App (right).
ByteDance
ByteDance
released an A2UI renderer for Lynx
, its cross-platform framework, in June 2026. Lynx keeps streamed screens smooth and ships a default set of components built on its `lynx-ui` library. In the
Lynx GenUI Playground
, you can watch A2UI messages rendered natively, for example, as a two-day trip planner for Kyoto. Lynx supports A2UI 0.9 today and is adapting to 1.0 with the A2UI team.
“A2UI is headed in the right direction: it separates how a model produces an interface from how an app renders it. Swappable inference formats and macros keep generation efficient, and even LLMs can be swapped for a System 1 model. In our playground, a decision model like Jev picks components and values instead of writing text, and then the SDK builds the A2UI screens that Lynx renders natively.”
-
Shouqun Liu
Engineering Lead for Lynx at ByteDance
Figure 3. In the Lynx GenUI Playground, A2UI messages (left) render natively in Lynx as a Kyoto trip planner (right).
Inside Google
Gemini Notebook
Ask Gemini Notebook for a slide deck and it replies with a card that asks two things: presenter slides or a detailed deck, and which topics to focus on. A review card follows with the format, focus, and visual style, which you can edit before it generates the deck. The same cards guide Video Overviews on the web and on mobile.
Figure 4. Gemini Notebook's options card (left) and review card (right).
Inside Gemini
Organizations can register their own agents that respond with A2UI. Gemini renders those responses using the components in its A2UI component gallery, and supports A2UI 0.9.1 today. The Google Cloud documentation covers
registering an agent
and hosting one on
Cloud Run
.
Several other Google teams, including some behind our largest products, are building features with A2UI.
Several other Google teams, including some behind our largest products, are building features with A2UI that haven’t launched yet. We’ll share more as they ship.
A2UI and MCP Apps
A2UI and MCP Apps work together. Alation already uses both to show its A2UI feeds in Claude. Our June post,
A2UI + MCP Apps
, covers three ways to combine them, and the
A2UI in MCP Apps guide
shows how to run A2UI screens inside an MCP App.
What's next
Jetpack Compose support for 1.0 is coming soon. Agents in
Gemini Enterprise
can already use A2UI, and we're working on upgrading Gemini Enterprise to A2UI 1.0. The
A2UI roadmap
covers the rest, from design-system primitives that render natively on every platform to official SDK support for decision models like Jev.
Get started
Read the docs and try the
quickstart
at
a2ui.org
.
Pick a renderer:
React
,
Angular
, and
Lit
on the web;
Flutter
on mobile, web, and desktop; and
SwiftUI
on iOS. The
Jetpack Compose
renderer supports 0.9.1 today, with 1.0 coming soon.
Upgrading from 0.9? The
evolution guide
covers every change.
File issues and discuss ideas at
github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui
Looking for Ideas?
We’ve collaborated with partners who have built A2UI 1.0 demos across different industries to give you inspiration on how to adapt A2UI to your use cases. Explore what they’ve built:
Homeward
(Real Estate and Moving Agent) by
Moonwise
Investing companion
(Finance and Investing Agent) by
Somnio Software
Alder
(Stylist Agent) by
L+R
;
GenUI Clinic
(Medical Records Agent) by
Solid Software
Riviera Home
(Smart Home Agent) by
Very Good Ventures
Vital Loop
(Vitals Tracker Agent) by
Oak Tree Apps
For one of the ways to run A2UI Express on a local or in-browser model, see the
Soverius AI
walkthrough
and
Gemma 4 fine-tuning article
.
Try your own ideas in
A2UI playground
by
Copilotkit
