Perplexity Decider v1.3: Training, eval, and use cases
See a demo
Try Perplexity
Perplexity Decider
How we train, evaluate, and use it.
Nov 12, 2026
Authors
Perplexity Research
We are releasing
Decider v1.3
and
Decider Flash v1.3
, the successors to our earlier decision models:
v1
,
v1.1
,
v1.2
, and
Flash v1.2
.
Decider Flash v1.3 is a smaller model distilled from Decider v1.3. Both models are available on
Hugging Face
under Apache license, through
OpenRouter
, and the
Perplexity Decisions API
.
Perplexity Decider is inspired by
Jev
, TypeSafe AIâs System One Model. It supports binary and multi-class classification with ordered or unordered labels, returning probabilities that applications can use to classify, route, rank, and evaluate inputs.
Both v1.3 models improve performance and robustness across a broad range of text and vision tasks through bidirectional attention, better-curated training data, and a refined training recipe. We also introduce
locate
, a new feature to highlight the selected content for named entity recognition, personal information identification, and extractive question-answering tasks.
In this post, we explain how we train and evaluate Decider and share how we use it internally at Perplexity.
What is a decision model?
A decision model is a general-purpose classifier. You give it an input and a set of questions each with its possible answers. For each question, it returns a probability distribution over the answers. It supports 3 question types:
Yes / No:
binary decisions.
Multiple choice:
custom multi-class labels.
Score:
ordered levels.
Decision models support a wide range of classification and scoring tasks:
Judging outputs:
assessing faithfulness, quality, and safety.
Routing:
directing requests to smaller or larger models based on difficulty.
Moderation and security:
detecting harmful content, phishing, and prompt injection in tool outputs.
Filtering and tagging:
organizing large collections of content.
Retrieval and reranking:
scoring search results by relevance.
Many of these tasks were previously handled by generative models like LLMs, even though they do not require free-form text generation. Decision models sit between LLMs and task-specific classifiers. They return probabilities for multiple questions about the same input in a single forward pass, avoiding token-by-token answer generation and sharing computation across questions. Unlike task-specific classifiers, they can handle new tasks through natural language prompts, a flexibility learned from training across diverse tasks in a shared question-answering format.
Training
Turning a generative LLM into a decision model
We build Decider by adapting strong generative LLM backbones. To explain the adaptation, we first describe how a request is represented. As illustrated below, a request consists out of a shared context (the state) and a number of questions. The state will be reused by all questions.
For example, given a document and its summary, a single request can ask whether the summary faithfully represents the document and whether it is intended for an expert or a general audience. After the state, each question block contains a question and its possible answers, each assigned a predefined label token such as A, B, or C. A special
<|marker|>
token indicates where to read out the modelâs prediction. At this position, a learned linear output layer (a decision head), maps the hidden state to scores for the questionâs answer options, which are then converted to probabilities.
Expand
We initialize the output layer from the base model, which normally scores next-token from the entire vocabulary, and only keep the rows corresponding to the predefined option tokens such as A, B, or C. This pruned layer is then trained to turn the hidden state of
<|marker|>
into answer scores. This approach covers all classification questions because they can all be formulated as a multiple choice.
For training, we take hundreds of public datasets spanning diverse tasks (sentiment, natural language inference, intent detection, entity matching, moderation, fact checking, ratings, etc.) and convert each example into the unified format described above: a state, one or more questions, their options and a target. The target can be the single correct option if we have gold labels, or a probability distribution over options.
In v1.3, we introduce
locate
, which extracts text from the state instead of selecting from predefined options. A locate question describes what to find, using either a short label such as âlocationâ or an instruction such as âExtract the city name where the job is located.â The model returns the exact matching text from the state, along with its start and end character locations. If it identifies no matches, it returns an empty list.
Expand
Because of shared state, a single request can combine locate, classification, and scoring questions about the same input. For example, it can ask whether a job requires senior-level experience and extract the required skills.
Bidirectional attention: letting the model read both ways
Our models start from strong pretrained generative backbones, whose causal attention lets each token attend only to itself and preceding tokens. Our ablation studies showed that making the backboneâs full-attention layers bidirectional improves performance, so we adopt this design to let each token incorporate context from the entire input.
Bidirectional attention introduces another design choice: how should the state and questions interact? We considered three attention patterns, with different implications for performance, answer stability, and cache reuse:
Everything sees everything (v1.2):
The state and all questions are processed together with full bidirectional attention. Computation over the state is shared, but an answer to one question can change depending on what else is asked.
Isolated questions (v1.3):
The state attends to all the questions, while each question attends only to the state and its own tokens. Questions can still influence one another indirectly through the shared state but results are more stable.
Fully cacheable:
The state only attends to itself, while each question attends to the state and its own tokens. The state is question-independent and reusable across requests to take advantage of prompt caching. We don't use it by default, because letting the state see the questions matters a lot for several tasks, but a small fine-tuning can switch a model to it.
We ultimately chose isolated questions for their strong performance and stability.
Expand
Training recipe
Training proceeds in three stages for both model sizes. We first train the larger model, based on
Qwen3.8-27B
, using cross-entropy on large datasets, then distill it into the smaller
Qwen3.5-4B
model.
The first stage is generalist training, where we fully fine-tune the model on large-scale corpora. In this stage, we only accept data that helps the model across the board and is not specific to any benchmark; we thus exclude any benchmark training splits.
After this generalist model is trained, we run a second, more fine-grained stage using
LoRA
. The data used in this stage is targeted toward specific domains and tasks. We add data in the second stage rather than the first one if we observe narrow gains or if we observe some regressions on other tasks. We use LoRA to avoid drifting too much from the generalist model and risking losing performance to fit those specific domains. The goal is to improve performance while retaining the backboneâs general knowledge. We also use a weight when merging the LoRA back into the base model, to control the drift more precisely and favor held-out metrics above any in-domain gains.
Finally, we add a vision-specific step. Similar to the second stage, the vision step is treated as another fine-grained specialization step, using a LoRA adapter that is merged back to the base model with a weight. Some vision capabilities can come at the price of text performance. Since we observe much more usage of the models on text, we prioritize text metrics over vision metrics.
For both text stages, we use the average weights from three runs, each using a different random seed. We found this improves the performance and robustness of the aggregated model.
Once the final large model is obtained, we apply the same three-stage training procedure to the smaller model. Here, the large model acts as the teacher: its predicted output distribution replaces the gold labels, and the smaller model is trained to minimize the KL divergence between its predictions and those of the teacher. This distillation objective outperforms cross-entropy on the same training data. While cross-entropy performs better on benchmarks with dedicated training data, it generalizes less well to held-out data. We hypothesize that distillation better transfers the teacherâs output distribution, including its confidence over non-gold alternatives, whereas cross-entropy encourages overfitting to the benchmark-specific training distribution. We therefore adopt the KL-based distillation objective.
To mitigate train-test contamination, we remove any training samples that could overlap with any evaluation we use. This is important because some public training datasets contain large parts of some evaluation datasets. We also conduct extensive bias audits and removal to make sure our gains are reliable and not just driven by learned biases.
Adding the ability to extract information
The locate
feature
extracts information such as named entities from text, without changing how it answers ordinary requests. To do so, we introduce an additional training stage: we add a new special token,
<|locate|>,
a span head, and LoRA adapter to Decider.
We initialize
<|locate|>
âs embedding from
<|marker|>
learned in the previous training stages. We train only this new embedding, the span head, and the LoRA adapters, while keeping the original backbone weights and decision head frozen. Each requested field gets its own
<|locate|>
token.
The span head uses
<|locate|>
âs representation together with the state-token representations to score where matching spans start and end, and which start-end pairs belong together. It also uses the
<|locate|>
tokenâs representation to predict field-specific thresholds for these scores. Selected spans are returned as character positions in the original text.
We train the span head with an adapted InfoNCE loss that pushes every gold span above the threshold, and the threshold above every other span. The loss has two terms: The first one pushes the scores of correct spans above the threshold and the wrong spans. The second term pushes the threshold above the scores of wrong spans. Fields with no answer get only the second term, which teaches the model to return an empty list.
We train on a mix of span extraction tasks, including named entity recognition, PII detection and extractive question answering. We vary the field descriptions from short labels to detailed instructions, so the model learns to follow the request rather than memorize a fixed label set.
Locate teaches the model a structurally different task, and we want to add it without losing what the model already does well. Merging the locate adapters into the backbone causes some regression on decision requests. To limit this, we are running investigations such as more replay data from earlier stages and auxiliary objectives that keep the modelâs outputs on decision requests close to those of the original model. However, we find that merging is currently still not lossless, so we keep the adapters unmerged and activate them only for locate requests.
Evaluation
We evaluate Decider v1.3 and Decider Flash v1.3 on external benchmarks from the
Hugging Face Decision Index
, Vals AIâs
ClaimBench
, and
Artificial Analysis Decision Index
.
Across these evaluations, our models demonstrate strong performance. Even though these leaderboards include privately held tasks, they can still be gamed through repeated submission and iterative tuning based on leaderboard feedback. To complement these leaderboards, we evaluate the models on an internal suite combining private production tasks with held-out evaluations drawn from public non-benchmark datasets. These evaluations provide an additional check on generalization beyond public benchmarks, helping us distinguish broader improvements from gains specific to familiar evaluation suites.
Internally, we built a suite of more than
200 tasks spanning various domains and tasks such as classification, scoring, reranking, and entity extraction. To honestly assess Deciderâs real-world performance, all evaluations are performed zero-shot, without task-specific fine-tuning, giving us a clear signal of where to improve the model.
Query classification
At Perplexity, we use a multi-head classification system to process each user query. Each query is first passed through an embedding model that acts as a feature extractor. The resulting embedding is then fed into multiple separate classification heads, including both binary and multi-label classifiers. For example, one head determines whether a user query should trigger web search.
Across 63 classification tasks with independently relabeled references by a frontier LLM, Decider v1.3 achieves 91.6% mean accuracy, exceeding our production classifiers by 6.54 percentage points. Decider Flash v1.3 also outperforms the production baseline, while Decider v1.3 outperforms Jev 1.14.
Expand
Domain-specific classification
We assembled a domain-specific evaluation suite from public datasets to assess decision modelsâ classification performance across seven domains: claim verification (6 tasks), healthcare (7), cybersecurity (8), programming (16), government (7), law (9) and finance (9).
For example, âjudge the time complexity of a Python programâ, or âuse an annual financial report to determine whether a companyâs unrestricted cash covers debt principal due within the next twelve monthsâ. Decider v1.3 leads across all seven domains, outperforming Jev 1.14 by up to 12.9 percentage points in finance and 9.3 points in law. Decider Flash v1.3 trails Jev 1.14 in finance, programming, and law, and performs similarly in other domains.
Expand
Retrieval and Reranking
Search is at the core of Perplexity. We maintain a broad suite of retrieval tasks to evaluate our modelsâ reranking performance. For each task, we first use a pool of embedding models to retrieve the top 50 candidate documents from each corpus. We then rerank these candidates using Decider and compare its performance against a strong reranker baseline, Qwen3-Reranker-8B.
We evaluate Decider in a zero-shot, pointwise setting, using the model to directly score each queryâdocument pair independently and rank documents by relevance. Across 72 retrieval tasks, Decider v1.3 achieves a mean nDCG@10 of 83.99, outperforming Qwen3-Reranker-8B by 1.81 points and Jev 1.14 by 2.24 points.
On the
BEIR benchmark
, both models outperform Qwen3-Reranker-8B by 8.78 and 7.05 nDCG@10 respectively. Against Jev 1.14, Decider v1.3 is 1.33 points higher, while the Flash version scores 0.4 lower.
Expand
Multilingual classification
To evaluate decision models beyond English, we assembled a multilingual classification benchmark comprising 19 language-specific tasks from 8 public datasets, with 46,484 examples across eight languages: German, Spanish, French, Italian, Russian, Japanese, Korean, and Chinese. The benchmark covers intent detection, topic classification, sentiment analysis, natural language inference, paraphrase detection, offensive language detection, and grammatical acceptability.
We report mean accuracy across tasks within each language, weighting each task equally. Decider v1.3 outperforms Jev 1.14 in all eight languages and Decider Flash v1.3 does so in six, with mean task accuracies of 88.16% for Decider v1.3 and 86.50% for Decider Flash v1.3, compared with 85.41% for Jev 1.14.
Expand
NER, PII and Extractive QA
We evaluate the locate feature on 17 out-of-domain tasks that test its extraction across various domains, input formats (text, tables, structured documents) and instructions (short labels, questions and detailed descriptions). The domains range from Wikipedia to scientific papers, cyber-threat reports, technical support, privacy policies, resumes, and legal contracts. The requests range from short label names such as âpersonâ or âemail addressâ, through questions about a table or a support ticket, to detailed field descriptions for structured extraction, such as the parties of an NDA or the total on an invoice.
We evaluate NER and PII using exact-span F1, which requires predicted spans to match the reference boundaries exactly. Extractive QA uses character-level F1, giving partial credit for overlapping answer text, while structured extraction uses field accuracy, the proportion of fields extracted correctly. For CV parsing, we average the NER and PII exact-span F1 scores.
We compare our models against general-purpose extraction models of different sizes: GLiNER large v2.5 (0.5B), Liquid d1 (2B) and Cloudflareâs Clairic (undisclosed). Decider v1.3 reaches an average score of 69.0 (using each taskâs primary metric) and Decider Flash v1.3 reaches 63.6, compared with 43.3 for Liquid d1, 41.5 for Clairic and 33.6 for GLiNER large v2.5. Both Decider models lead in every category.
Expand
Image classification
Decider has natively supported vision tasks since v1. To evaluate its performance beyond text, we assembled a five-task benchmark suite with a particular focus on document classification, including invoices, letters, and resumes. The suite also covers satellite image classification, texture classification, pet breed classification, and animal counting.
Decider v1.3 achieves a mean accuracy of 76.99% across the five visual tasks, outperforming Jev 1.14 by 1.47 percentage points. Decider Flash v1.3 achieves 72.77%, demonstrating visual classification capabilities in a smaller model.
Expand
Real-world decision requests
We sampled one million deduplicated, PII-masked requests submitted to the Perplexity Decision API during its first 18 days of availability. Because each request can contain multiple questions about the same state, the sample comprises 2,318,887 individual questions. All requests were included with explicit user permission for research.
Production requests do not come with ground-truth labels, so we use frontier LLM judges to generate reference answers and measure each modelâs agreement with them. We also group the requests into 10 task categories, including information extraction, domain classification, sentiment analysis, intent and routing, relevance ranking, content moderation, quality and compliance review, entity matching, business analysis, and an âOtherâ category. This breakdown shows how performance varies across real-world use cases.
The task mix is uneven: information extraction accounts for 425,402 questions, domain classification for 409,564, and sentiment analysis for 344,158. Together, these three categories make up 50.8% of the sampled questions.
Decider v1.3 achieves the highest agreement with the judges at 93.98%, compared with 93.68% for Decider v1.2 and 93.35% for Jev 1.14. Decider v1.3 and Jev 1.14 are closely matched on domain classification and sentiment analysis, with gaps of 0.34 and 0.07 percentage points, respectively. Jev leads by 0.69 points on relevance ranking, while Decider v1.3 leads by 0.93 points on information extraction (the most common task in the sample) and by 1.21 points on intent and routing.
Expand
The chart below compares the reported cost of running the same one million production requests. Each request can contain multiple questions, so the unit here is requests, not individual questions.
Expand
Decider ran locally; GLM and DeepSeek used llm-api; Jev used OpenRouter. Reported costs are workload-specific, with unspecified local hardware-cost accounting and no matched latency comparison.
Robustness
We evaluated label sensitivity on 372 multiple-choice questions, making 4,788 requests per model. We reordered options, reassigned labels to answer texts, and renamed labels while preserving each questionâs meaning, then checked whether the modelâs semantic answer changed. Lower flip rates indicate greater stability.
Decider v1.3 changed its answer on just 0.27% of questions under each transformation, compared with 2.69â4.84% for Jev 1.14. We also repeated identical inputs to measure serving variability: Decider v1.3 showed no changes, while Jev 1.14 changed on 1.88% of questions.
Expand
How we use Decider
Decider is built for workflows that need fast and structured decisions. In this section we explore how to leverage them to produce meaningful impact on the way we work. Here are some that stood out.
Self-improving security rules
Internally, we are already using Decider to improve our security policies.
The activity of our agents is recorded and a series of rule-based checks are performed to identify any problematic behavior. A rule-based approach means that we can monitor our agents in real-time with negligible latency added. Offline, we use Decider to look at samples from these recorded agent logs. In the case that no problematic behavior was flagged, Decider checks if there is something that our set of rules missed; and in the case that an alarm was raised, Decider checks whether this was a false alarm. Any records where our rule set fails in either case are sent to an agent for triage and a fix to the rules is proposed, to be approved by a member of our security team.
In one day, Decider read 1 billion tokens across 7,000 agent sessions and identified flaws that led to 14 rule fixes, 6 of which were approved and shipped within two days. Replayed on a week of logs, the fixes cut our busiest rule's volume by 52%, and the widened rules caught about 40% more legitimate actions to investigate.
Expand
Monitoring RL rollouts
When we post-train models with reinforcement learning, aggregate metrics such as a terminal reward do not explain why a rollout (an individual attempt at a task) succeeded or failed. It can lose reward unfairly because a tool service or the sandbox failed, or receive undeserved reward if the evaluator overlooks an unsupported claim, such as a made-up value that no tool returned.
We use Decider to monitor rollouts for these cases. Code first identifies parts of a rollout that warrant closer inspection: a failed tool call and the surrounding reasoning, code that ran without errors, or the final answer. Decider then answers multiple-choice questions about each part, such as what failed in a step (a tool service, an external site, the sandbox, the harness, or the agentâs own code) and whether the agent interpreted the result correctly. We bundle all questions about a given part into a single request and store the probabilities rather than a verdict, so we can adjust thresholds later without querying Decider again. The monitor only observes and diagnoses: it never changes a reward or stops a run.
Expand
Page quality filtering
When crawling web pages to index and serve to users, many pages are too low quality to be of any use. This includes anti-bot walls, CAPTCHAs, and error pages, as well as correctly loaded web pages that just donât contain any helpful information, such as spam, SEO filler or navigation-only pages. These low-quality pages need to be identified and filtered out of our index.
Using Decider, we can judge the quality of pages as we crawl them. In the same forward pass, we perform a suite of other classification tasks such as identifying the domain and intended audience of the content and whether it contains harmful, illegal, or personally identifiable information. Compared to using an LLM judge, Decider is considerably faster and cheaper.
Expand
Illustrative page-quality request: Useful information, intended audience, harmful or illegal content, and personally identifiable information are assessed from the same page.
Beyond these internal uses, Decider also fits workflows such as the following.
Visual QA
Because Decider reads images, it also works as a visual checker, reviewing style changes to web pages or apps and identifying faults. It can review page screenshots for clipped text, overlapping elements, broken layouts before a change ships, or flag charts whose design could mislead a reader or break a brand guide.
Expand
Browser navigation
Agents can use Decider for the small decisions inside larger tasks. A browser agent can send a screenshot at each step and receive detailed information about the state of the page and the expected outcome of each possible action.
Expand
Planning research tasks
Usersâ questions can greatly vary in their complexity, as does the depth of search that needs to be performed to find an answer. Decider can estimate this before search begins, allowing for fewer resources to be spent on simple questions.
Expand
Getting started
Decider returns probabilities. The appropriate decision threshold depends on the application. Label frequencies and the relative costs of false positives and false negatives vary across use cases. We therefore encourage users to tune thresholds on a small, representative labeled development set rather than assume that a fixed cutoff will work equally well across tasks.
We recommend using Decider v1.3 for nuanced judgments, detailed rubrics, and workflows where errors are costly. Choose Decider Flash v1.3 for high-volume routing, labeling, and filtering where latency and cost are the main constraints. Evaluate both models on representative examples from your workload, then choose the model that meets your quality, latency, and budget requirements.
Both models are available as downloadable weights on
Hugging Face
under Apache license, through
OpenRouter
, and the
Perplexity Decisions API
.

Cohere Expands Its Sovereign AI Platform with AISLE and cubic
Expanding the sovereign AI platform with new capabilities for cyber defense, secure software development, and mission-critical enterprise workflows
Blog
Written By
Cohere Team
Tags
Company News
Sovereign AI
Share
AI isn’t a shortcut.
It’s how business gets ahead.
Contact sales
Over the past year, we've seen a fundamental shift in how organizations approach AI. Enterprises and governments are deploying AI into the workflows that matter most, from cybersecurity and software development to mission-critical operations and decision-making. As they do, their requirements are becoming increasingly clear: they need AI systems that are powerful, secure, and under their control.
At Cohere, we've long believed organizations shouldn't have to choose between cutting-edge AI and control. They should be able to deploy advanced AI while maintaining ownership of their data, infrastructure, and operations. That's the foundation of sovereign AI.
Today, we're excited to share two important milestones in that journey. We're pleased to announce the completion of our acquisition of AISLE, the company building autonomous systems for vulnerability discovery and remediation. We're also welcoming the team behind cubic, one of the leading AI-powered code review platforms, to Cohere.
Together, these additions strengthen the sovereign AI platform we're building for organizations around the world. With
AISLE
and cubic we’ve completed four strategic M&A transactions this year, following
Aleph Alpha
,
Reliant AI
to expand our capabilities across frontier AI, biopharma and healthcare, cybersecurity, and software development.
Cybersecurity is a defining frontier of AI
As AI becomes embedded in critical systems and workflows, security is becoming a defining requirement for adoption. Organizations increasingly need AI that can operate inside private clouds, on-premises and air-gapped environments while meeting rigorous requirements around privacy, governance, and compliance.
That's why we're excited to officially welcome AISLE to Cohere. When we announced our intent to acquire AISLE, we outlined a shared belief: the future of AI depends on the ability to secure both AI systems and the software infrastructure that powers them. As organizations deploy AI into increasingly sensitive environments, cyber resilience becomes foundational to trust.
AISLE’s co-founders are taking leadership roles spanning cybersecurity, corporate security, AI security research and frontier model development. Ondrej Vlcek will become Senior Vice President, Cohere Cyber, and lead the newly established cybersecurity business. Jaya Baloo will become Cohere’s Chief Information Security Officer, overseeing security across the company. Stanislav Fort will become Vice President, AI Security, joining Cohere’s core model research and training efforts while leading AI security research.
Cohere also plans to make a substantial long-term investment in Prague, expanding AISLE’s existing presence and establishing the city as its global center for AI cybersecurity and autonomous security systems.
AISLE brings world-class expertise in autonomous security research and vulnerability discovery.
Their work has demonstrated how specialized AI systems can identify, validate, and remediate vulnerabilities at a speed and scale that helps defenders stay ahead of an increasingly complex threat landscape.
Today, that expertise has become the foundation of Cohere Cyber, our cybersecurity business focused on helping enterprises, governments, and critical infrastructure operators build and operate secure, cyber-resilient AI systems. Together, we're building cyber defense capabilities that help organizations deploy AI with confidence in even the most demanding environments.
Bringing secure coding to enterprise scale
Software development is one of the most widely adopted enterprise applications of AI. But organizations need more than systems that generate code. They need AI that can understand complex codebases, review changes, identify vulnerabilities, maintain software quality, and operate within strict security boundaries. That's what attracted us to cubic.
The team has built an industry-leading AI-powered code review platform that helps engineering organizations review code, find bugs and vulnerabilities, understand complex codebases, and automatically remediate issues. Their review agents have consistently ranked among the strongest performers on code review benchmarks and were built for the environments many enterprise customers operate in, including on-premises and air-gapped deployments.
Led by founder and CEO Paul Sanglé-Ferrière, the team brings expertise across AI, security, developer tools, distributed systems, and enterprise software. They will establish Cohere's secure coding vertical, helping accelerate the integration of enterprise-grade coding capabilities into our platform while meeting the security, governance, and deployment requirements our customers demand. Their work strengthens our ability to help organizations build, maintain, and secure software using AI within their own environments and under their own control.
Building AI for the world's most critical industries
What connects AISLE and cubic is more than technical excellence. Both teams have built products for organizations operating in environments where security, reliability, governance, and control are non-negotiable.
Their work reflects a broader shift we're seeing across the market. Organizations increasingly want AI they can deploy on their own terms. They want systems that fit within their security requirements, regulatory obligations, and operational realities without becoming dependent on systems they can't inspect, adapt, or control.
We believe this is where the next phase of AI adoption will be won. By bringing together frontier models, secure deployment infrastructure, cyber defense, and purpose-built applications, we're continuing to build a sovereign AI platform that gives organizations more capability, more security, and more control.
Looking ahead
The future of AI won't be defined by models alone. It will be defined by the systems, workflows, and infrastructure built around them. The question is whether organizations can deploy AI securely and at scale across the systems that matter most. That's the promise of sovereign AI.
Welcoming AISLE and cubic to Cohere strengthens our ability to deliver on that vision. Together, we're building a sovereign AI platform that enterprises and governments can trust to operate in their most sensitive environments, power their most critical workflows, and realize the full potential of AI while maintaining control of their data, infrastructure, and operations.
We're excited to welcome both teams to Cohere and look forward to what we'll build together.

We

Kitesurf
, our stateless browser for AI agents that runs entirely on top of Workers, in August and
followed up
Â in September with WebMCP support, new APIs, and improved compatibility. On every occasion, we mentioned our commitment to open sourcing it so that developers could run their own browser engine on their own Cloudflare accounts if they want to.
That promise is now real.
Kitesurf is open source on GitHub
Â under the Apache 2.0 license.Â You can read the code, run it locally, change it, and deploy your own instance to Cloudflare Workers.
A browser built for agents
Kitesurf runs entirely on Cloudflare Workers. It parses HTML, applies CSS, executes page JavaScript, and renders screenshots without a browser container. It supports the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), so you can connect clients such as Puppeteer.
Our main goal is to give AI agents a lightweight, efficient browser â one that can load websites, execute JavaScript, and interact with pages while using less CPU and memory than a full browser like Chromium, and scaling on demand across Cloudflareâs global Workers network.
Read more about why and how we built Kitesurf in our initial
announcement
Â and how to use it in Browser Runâs
developer
Â documentation.
What is inside the repository?
Kitesurf builds on Cloudflareâs Developer Platform and APIs, alongside an ecosystem of open-source Rust packages compiled to WebAssembly:
Blitz
Â provides HTML parsing, the DOM, layout, and painting.
Stylo
Â provides CSS parsing, cascading, and computed styles.
Boa
Â runs JavaScript inside WebAssembly (as the last resort only when we canât run JavaScript in Dynamic Workers).
Linebender
Â libraries provide text layout and 2D graphics, and
Krilla
Â generates PDF output.
These projects made Kitesurf possible. They retain their respective licenses; the repository's
NOTICE
Â documents third-party notices.
Kitesurf has three main parts: the Engine manages browser sessions and client connections, PageScript runs the page and its JavaScript, and PageRenderer draws the result.
All packages, the engine, its Rust core, DOM shims, renderer, and
Kitesurf CLI
Â live separately in folders under the repositoryâs
packages
Â directory where you can explore how all the pieces fit together.
Run your own Kitesurf
To run Kitesurf locally, follow the repository's
build requirements
, then clone the
repository
, install dependencies, and start the engine:
git
clone
https://github.com/cloudflare/kitesurf.git
cd
kitesurf
pnpm
install
--frozen-lockfile
pnpm
run
dev
The first build compiles the Rust core and its dependencies, so give it some time. Subsequent builds reuse the build cache. Finally wrangler starts a local development server at
http://127.0.0.1:8787
. Open that address to try a page in Chrome DevTools, or use it programmatically.
You can use
puppeteer
Â with a NodeJS script:
import
puppeteer
from
"puppeteer-core"
;
const
browser
=
await
puppeteer.
connect
({
browserWSEndpoint:
"ws://127.0.0.1:8787/devtools/browser"
,
});
try
{
const
page
=
await
browser.
newPage
();
await
page.
goto
(
"https://example.com/"
);
await
page.
screenshot
({ path:
"page.png"
});
}
finally
{
await
browser.
disconnect
();
}
Or you can point your AI harness at the local
CDP
Â port (agents love CDP) and watch it take full control of Kitesurf.
Deploy to your Cloudflare account
When youâre done changing and testing locally, you can
deploy the engine to your own account
Â and use Kitesurf from there instead of the Browser Run managed APIs we provide. Note that a Workers Paid plan is required because Kitesurf uses
Dynamic Workers
Â to create isolated Workers for pages.
From the repository root:
pnpm run deploy
Help us make it better
As with all of our open-sourced projects, Kitesurf lives in Github and we welcome forks and
contributions
.Â However, note that Kitesurf is under heavy development and we are focusing on making the engine more compatible (check out
Web Platform Test evolution
), more reliable, and
efficient
.
Start with the
contribution guidelines
Â if you want to contribute. Open an issue with a minimal reproduction or a proposed approach, and get vouched by a maintainer before opening a pull request. Focused fixes with tests, clear evidence, and a well-defined scope are much easier to review than large rewrites or unrelated cleanup, but all contribution does not have to be code: a small page that reproduces a rendering bug, a failing automation workflow, or a clear documentation correction can help us move forward.
Stay tuned
Kitesurf is evolving quickly. Stay tuned for updates in the
blog
Â and our
changelog
, and keep an eye on the official
landing page
Â for the latest on standards compatibility in
Web Platform Tests
Â page and
benchmarks
.
And come chat with the team on
Discord
. Weâre building a browser for agents, and weâd love your help making it better.

Accelerating the agentic era: How Arm and ​​Google​ Cloud co-design​ infrastructure for TPU 8i Max
Arm-based Google Axion host processors​​ extend their role across Google’s TPU ​​​portfolio to deliver the high performance and energy efficiency required for demanding AI workloads.
Share
Google Cloud is pairing​​ ​one of ​its newest TPU system​s​ ​with​ ​Google Axion processors that are custom
Arm Neoverse®
-based CPUs​. With TPU 8i Max, Google is extending its use of Axion CPUs as the host compute for its AI accelerators, building on Axion’s role in TPU 8t and TPU 8i.
​​Google Axion provides the CPU foundation to support Google’s AI infrastructure across large-scale training, real-time reasoning, and increasingly demanding agentic workloads. Google’s expansion to TPU 8i Max marks another significant milestone for Arm at the heart of the systems powering next-generation AI infrastructure.
Advancing performance across the AI system
AI performance depends on more than the accelerator. CPUs prepare data, orchestrate workloads and execute the infrastructure software that keeps the entire system productive. As agents reason, use tools and coordinate complex tasks, the demands on that CPU foundation continue to grow.
With Axion, Google brings together Neoverse performance and efficiency with custom silicon designed for its infrastructure. Extending that approach to TPU 8i Max reinforces the importance of the CPU and accelerator co-design in scaling AI.
Arm Neoverse-based Axion CPUs as host compute for TPU 8t, TPU 8i, and TPU 8i Max
“Delivering AI performance at scale requires​ co-designing​ CPUs and accelerators ​to work​ seamlessly​ together,” said Mark Lohmeyer, VP & GM, AI and Computing Infrastructure​​, Google Cloud. “​Our ​Arm-based Google Axion ​processors deliver ​​​the performance, efficiency and flexibility​ required​ to ​​power​ the demanding host workloads behind our TPU systems. With TPU 8i Max, we’re extending that ​co-designed ​foundation to​ help customers tackle their most complex AI applications.”
Unlocking the age of inference
Google Cloud’s continued investment reflects a broader industry shift toward pairing CPUs with accelerators to unlock the next era of AI inference.​ Beyond serving as accelerator host compute, Google Axion also powers general-purpose cloud instances that run agent runtimes and orchestration frameworks.​
Earlier this year, Google Cloud announced
Google Axion N4A
, which delivers up to 2x better price-performance than comparable current-generation x86-based virtual machines. With
GKE Agent Sandbox
running on Axion N4A, customers can also securely isolate agentic AI workloads while achieving 30% better price-performance.​ Building on this momentum, Agent Substrate on GKE also natively supports Google Axion processors, providing an open-source, secure-by-default agent execution runtime engineered to run millions of sandboxes with 10x higher density than standard container runtimes.​
From powering Google’s latest TPU systems to enabling millions of AI agents to operate at scale, Arm is helping build the compute foundation for the next era of AI.

For AI Advice to Be Any Good, It Has to Actually Change the Outcome
Real-time AI video assistants need a new kind of test. Here’s how we built the necessary proving ground.
Honglu Zhou
Manager, Salesforce AI Research
Shelby Heinecke
Director, Salesforce AI Research
Silvio Savarese
Executive Vice President and Chief Scientist, Salesforce AI Research
November 12, 2026
5 min read
A technician kneels beside a commercial water heater, phone propped against a pipe, an
AI assistant
watching through the camera. She reaches for the wrong valve and the assistant says, “Stop, that’s the supply line.” Whether that counts as useful guidance depends entirely on what happens next. Did the warning arrive in time to prevent an incorrect action? Did she trust it? Did it confuse her about the next step?
Those questions are about to matter much more. AI assistants are leaving the chat window and becoming real-time guides for physical work, watching live video and instructing people through multistep tasks.
The frontier moved quickly this year. In May,
Thinking Machines
previewed interaction models that continuously take in audio, video, and text and respond in real time, rather than waiting for a user to finish a turn. In June,
Meta
researchers released a wearable video dataset for proactive procedural assistance, annotated for moments when users go off plan and how to recover.
In September,
Google introduced Gemini 3.8 Live
, combining real-time visual understanding, spoken conversation, and the ability to work on tasks in the background.
But there’s a catch: Most evaluations of visual assistants replay prerecorded video and grade responses against an answer key. That tells you whether a warning was correct. It can’t tell you whether the warning worked, because a recording can’t react.
So
Salesforce AI Research
built
Interactive Visual Gym
, a simulated proving ground where AI assistants coach virtual workers that can react to instructions. That way, researchers can see whether the advice actually changes the outcome, develop benchmarks, and ultimately improve these visual assistants.
The feedback loop of a live trial, but at scale
A leader deciding whether to give a visual AI assistant to frontline teams wants to know if those teams are more likely to finish the job, and finish it correctly, with the assistant than without it.
The obvious approach is to test with real people, but that doesn’t scale. Knowing whether an assistant reliably helps technicians would take thousands of training runs with people of different skill levels, making different mistakes at different moments. Recruiting that many participants for every device and procedure would be slow and prohibitively expensive. What’s needed is the feedback loop of a live trial at the scale of a dataset.
That’s what Interactive Visual Gym provides. IVG recreates everyday physical tasks like cooking or managing smartphone settings. It pairs each task with a simulated user performing the task while receiving guidance from the visual AI assistant. The simulated user’s actions and the simulated environment change in response to this guidance.
In a kitchen environment, for example, a simulated cook works through a recipe like assembling a burger: one bun, then the patty, then the cheese. If it grabs the wrong ingredient, the AI assistant watching has to catch the mistake in time so the cook can react to whatever it says.
Three design choices make IVG practical. First, the AI assistants speak in natural language (“go to the pan with the meat”), not in the joint velocities and degree coordinates of classical robotics simulators. Second, we can schedule out-of-plan moments at precise points in a task while keeping the user’s dialogue consistent with its behavior. These include mistakes, mid-task plan changes, questions, and reminder requests. Third, simulated users vary along four axes: skill, trust in AI, preferred execution speed, and tolerance for interruption. A seasoned user who wants to be left alone and a novice who wants every step spelled out need very different help.
Related
Salesforce Releases R&D Agents That Improve Its AI Models
5 min read
New Data Shows Sales Agents Are Rescuing the Sales Cycle
4 min read
What today’s assistants get wrong, and how IVG can help
Using IVG, we built IVG-Bench: 315 scenarios across three environments, used to evaluate 15 assistants each running on a different model. The strongest, running on Gemini 4 Argon, completed only 53.4% of tasks within the time limit, averaged across environments, and open-weight models generally trailed the leading frontier models. This is still a challenging benchmark to achieve.
Our dynamic evaluation exposes several problems with AI visual assistants. The first is that a model can help users finish more often but might actually give clumsier advice along the way, so we need two metrics to measure capability: task success and interaction quality. The second is that dynamic testing exposes failures that static tests miss. Latency turns correct advice into stale advice. Telling the user to approach the table after the user has already arrived there is pointless. Some assistants repeat instructions the user has already acknowledged. For some open-weight models, guidance degrades as the task goes on.
To check that our simulation-based scores reflect real experience, we had people control the cook in the simulator, work with different assistants, and rank them. When people preferred one assistant over another, our automated interaction-quality score from the simulation corresponded to their preference 78.5% of the time. Real people and simulated users also behaved similarly, with one difference: Simulated users speak and reply far more often.
Our simulated environments can also actively improve the performance of visual assistants. In an early proof of concept, we used the simulator to train an open-source model, incentivizing it to prioritize task completion and error prevention. The model’s success rate improved and the assistant became noticeably better at delivering the right advice at the right time, stepping in proactively before mistakes happened.
What this means for leaders
Ultimately, real-time visual assistants will be judged by outcomes. Before deploying one, ask three things: Does it measurably help people finish the task? Does its guidance arrive while it can still change the outcome? Does it hold up deep into a long job, or when the user goes off script? Answering those questions means testing the interaction itself, in environments where advice has consequences. That’s what Interactive Visual Gym is built to do.
